claude.sample_unit: online participants (analog patients) rating one response each

links.outcome: Effect of perceived AI vs physician authorship label on ratings of empathy, quality, trust
links.effect: Responses believed to be physician-authored were rated higher in empathy regardless of actual source (perceived-source main effect ηp2 = 0.17, p < 0.001). Trust ηp2 = 0.25. Disclosure of AI authorship lowered perceived empathy and trust.
links.quote: Importantly, having information about who authored the response mattered, as participants rated responses they believed to be from a physician higher in empathy than responses they believed to be generated by a chatbot, regardless of the actual source of the response.

links.outcome: Empathy of ChatGPT vs physician responses to patient questions, rated by participants and coded for language elements
links.effect: Chatbot responses rated more empathic than physician responses (M = 3.25 vs 2.60, d = 0.56, p < 0.001). Chatbot responses had more validation, reassurance and non-judgmental language and appeared less hurried.
links.quote: Actual chatbot responses ( M = 3.25, SD = 0.80) were rated higher in empathy than actual physician responses ( M = 2.60, SD = 0.76), t (63) = 4.51, p < 0.001, d = 0.56 (Appendix B eTable 3 ).

unlisted_practices: Coding verbal elements of AI responses (validation, reassurance, active listening) to identify what drives perceived empathy
Using AI-augmented messaging to teach clinicians empathic communication phrases

links.outcome: user reactions to AI source disclosure
links.effect: Perceived physician authorship increased empathy ηp2=0.17, p<0.001; trust followed same pattern, ηp2=0.25, p<0.001.
links.quote: Empathy ratings were higher when participants thought the response was physician-authored, whether it was or not (η<sub>p</sub><sup>2 </sup>= 0.17, p < 0.001).

links.effect: Chatbot responses had more empathic elements and were less rushed/more structured; Cohen’s d=0.32 to 1.82, p’s<0.01.
links.quote: Chatbot responses contained more coder-rated validation, reassurance, and non-judgmental language and were less rushed and more structured than physician responses (Cohen's d = 0.32 to 1.82, p's < 0.01).

links.outcome: Perceived empathy, trust, quality, liking, and goodness by attributed source
links.effect: Believed physician authorship increased ratings for empathy (ηp2=0.17, p<0.001), trust (ηp2=0.25, p<0.001), goodness (ηp2=0.16, p<0.01), liking (ηp2=0.11, p<0.01), and quality (ηp2=0.10, p<0.05) versus believed chatbot authorship.
links.quote: Responses that participants believed had come from a physician were rated as more empathic regardless of the actual source.

links.outcome: Coder-rated verbal empathy and communication elements
links.effect: Chatbot responses had more validation (d=0.79), active listening (d=1.57), structured guidance (d=1.38), non-judgmental language (d=0.84), collaborative language (d=1.56), and appeared less rushed (d=-1.82) than physician responses (all p<0.01).
links.quote: Chatbot responses contained significantly more of every coded behavior compared to physician responses except for medical jargon, for which there was no significant difference, and appearing hurried or rushed for which physician responses were rated higher than chatbot responses (Table 4 ).

screen.practice: disclosure of AI authorship to patients
screen.reason: The study directly tests how patient perceptions (empathy, trust, quality) change depending on whether responses are disclosed/labeled as AI-generated vs. physician-authored (evaluating disclosure/labeling effects).

primary.practice: AI disclosure / framing source of response to patients
